explanations.answer: Without passing judgment on his opinions
explanations.explanation: Verse 1 says it plainly: “Accept him whose faith is weak, without passing judgment on his opinions.” No clipboard, no pop quiz at the door. You open the door and let him in. I think plenty of people breathe easier hearing that.

Paul doesn't set that condition. He says to accept him “…without passing judgment on his opinions.” The acceptance comes first, and it doesn't wait for a makeover. Imagine telling a cookie to bake itself before you'll let it in the oven.

explanations.answer: Only once his faith grows stronger
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't tell them to wait. He says, “Accept him whose faith is weak…” so the welcome goes to the weak one right now. Nobody hangs a sign on a bakery door that says come back when you're stronger. I'd lose every customer by lunch.

Easy to read it that way, but look at verse 2. Paul says one person “…has faith to eat all things, while another, who is weak, eats only vegetables.” The word weak lands on the vegetable eater. Paul never hangs that label on the one who eats all things.

Right. Verse 2 says one person “…has faith to eat all things…” and the word weak goes to the other one, who “…eats only vegetables.” Paul doesn't call the eater of everything weak. Good thing, because I'd still be sulking if somebody had called me weak in my own bakery.

Yes, the verse ends with “…for God has accepted him.” That's the reason the one who doesn't eat everything must not judge the one who does. If God has already accepted him, who's left to hand out a rejection slip? Not me, friend.

Paul doesn't say God has warned him. He says God has accepted him. That's the reason the one who doesn't eat everything must not judge the one who does. A warning would sound like a stern letter, and this verse sounds like an open door.

Paul doesn't say tested here. The word is accepted: “…for God has accepted him.” So the one who doesn't eat everything has no reason to judge the one who does. God's acceptance is already settled, and no taste test is coming.

Yes, “To his own master he stands or falls.” Paul's picture is a servant and his master, and the master is the one whose opinion counts. Everybody else in the room is just watching. Watching is a lot easier than being the boss, friend.

Close, but Paul doesn't say teacher. He says the servant stands or falls “To his own master…” A servant answers to the one he serves, so the master is the one who decides. Nobody in the stands gets a vote.

Paul doesn't use the word king here. The servant stands or falls “To his own master…” It's a servant and master picture, and the point is that the judging belongs to the master. It doesn't belong to whoever happens to be standing nearby with an opinion.

Yes. Paul says, “And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.” The servant's standing doesn't depend on whoever is judging him. It depends on the Lord. That's good news for anybody who's ever been sized up by somebody with a very strong opinion.
Paul doesn't name elders. He says “…the Lord is able to make him stand.” The one who holds him up is the same Lord he answers to. Elders do plenty of good, but Paul isn't giving them this job.

Paul doesn't say friends. The one able to make him stand is “the Lord.” Friends are great for a ride to the airport, but this verse puts the holding up in the Lord's hands. That's a firmer place for the servant to be.

Yes, “Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.” Paul wants each person settled in his own thinking about the day he keeps. Convictions are meant to be walked out before the Lord, and not borrowed from the loudest voice around. Borrowing someone else's certainty is like wearing their apron: it never quite fits.

Paul says each one should be fully convinced in his own mind, not in his family. The conviction is meant to sit in the person himself. It isn't handed down like a cookie jar on a shelf. Family can be wonderful, but this verse points inward.

Paul doesn't say village. The word is mind: “…fully convinced in his own mind.” So the settling happens inside the person, and a crowd doesn't do it for him. If a whole village could settle it, nobody would ever need to think.

explanations.answer: They do it to the Lord
explanations.explanation: Yes. Paul says the one who keeps a special day, the one who eats and the one who abstains each do it “…to the Lord…” Three different choices, and the same direction. The thing they share is who they're doing it to.

explanations.answer: They do it to please others
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. He says each of them does it “…to the Lord…” The one who keeps a day, the one who eats and the one who abstains are all aimed at Him. Pleasing the crowd isn't the common thread in this verse.

explanations.answer: They do it to earn God's favor
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that here. What he says is that each one does it “…to the Lord…” The verse also mentions that the eater and the one who abstains give thanks to God. Thanks is a different thing from earning, friend.

Yes. Verse 6 says, “…he who abstains does so to the Lord and gives thanks to God.” So the one who skips certain foods is still thanking God. That's why this isn't a contest between the eaters and the skippers.

Paul says the opposite. Verse 6 says, “…he who abstains does so to the Lord and gives thanks to God.” The one who skips a food still gives thanks. It's an easy thing to miss, but Paul wants us to see it.
Yes. Verse 8 says, “So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.” Notice it covers both living and dying. Nobody belongs to a rumor, a rule list or a cookie jar, friend. We belong to the Lord.

Listening is a good thing, but it isn't Paul's word here. He says, “So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.” Belonging goes deeper than listening. It's about whose we are, in life and in death.

Praying is good, but Paul's word is belong. Verse 8 says, “So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.” It isn't about something we do. It's about whose we are, and that holds whether we live or die.

explanations.answer: To be Lord of both the dead and the living
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 9 says Christ died and returned to life “…that He might be the Lord of both the dead and the living.” That's a huge reach. It covers the people here now and the people already gone. Everybody Paul has been talking about already belongs to Him.

explanations.answer: To settle every dispute over food
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give that reason. He says Christ died and returned to life “…that He might be the Lord of both the dead and the living.” That's far bigger than a dispute over food. It makes Him the Lord of everyone in the argument.

explanations.answer: To make one day holier than the rest
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. He says Christ died and returned to life “…that He might be the Lord of both the dead and the living.” His purpose is Lordship over people, living and dead. It isn't about ranking the days on a calendar.

explanations.answer: We will all stand before God's judgment seat
explanations.explanation: Yes. Paul says, “For we will all stand before God’s judgment seat.” Notice the word all. That includes the person doing the judging. I think that tends to quiet the room fast.

explanations.answer: The apostles will sort it all out
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. His reason is, “For we will all stand before God’s judgment seat.” The one who judges is God, and the apostles aren't mentioned. So the one doing the judging has no seat on that bench.

explanations.answer: Others will only judge us back
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give that reason. He says, “For we will all stand before God’s judgment seat.” The reason to stop is that we all stand before God. It has nothing to do with dodging payback.

Yes. Verse 12 says, “So then, each of us will give an account of himself to God.” Each person reports for himself. You don't turn in a report on somebody else's batch, friend. Mine is plenty to keep track of.
Paul says it the other way around. Each of us will give an account “…of himself to God.” The account is about our own life. Nobody is handed a brother's paperwork to cover.
Paul doesn't say neighbor. Verse 12 says each of us will give an account “…of himself to God.” It's our own account, and not someone else's. So there's no need to keep tabs on the neighbor's batch.

explanations.answer: Not to put a stumbling block in a brother's way
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 13 says, “…make up your mind not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in your brother’s way.” The energy that used to go into judging goes into keeping his path clear. Think of it like a hallway. Nobody wants to leave a box in the middle of it for someone else to trip over.

explanations.answer: Not to share a meal with a weaker brother
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. He says, “…make up your mind not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in your brother’s way.” Nothing in the verse tells them to stay away from each other. It's about what they put in his path.

explanations.answer: Not to bring up special days ever again
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. The thing to make up their minds about is, “…not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in your brother’s way.” It's about the way they treat each other. Special days aren't banned from conversation.

Yes. Paul says, “But if anyone regards something as unclean, then for him it is unclean.” He has just said he's convinced nothing is unclean in itself. Even so, he treats the other person's conviction with respect. That's the twist.

Paul does say it. Verse 14 reads, “But if anyone regards something as unclean, then for him it is unclean.” Right before that he says nothing is unclean in itself. The two go together, and the second part keeps us gentle with the person who sees it differently.

Yes. Paul says, “…you are no longer acting in love.” He's talking about what happens when your brother is distressed by what you eat. Love sets how you eat. Hunger doesn't, and neither does being right.

Wisdom is a good thing, but Paul's word is love. He says that if your brother is distressed by what you eat, “…you are no longer acting in love.” The test is love, not who's the smartest at the table.

Truth matters, but that isn't Paul's word here. He says, “…you are no longer acting in love.” The question he asks is whether your eating is loving toward your brother. Being technically correct about the food doesn't settle it.
Yes. Paul says, “…your brother, for whom Christ died.” That's how much that brother matters. If Christ died for him, I'm not going to let a snack outrank him.

explanations.answer: He will judge you one day
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that about the brother. He says, “…your brother, for whom Christ died.” The weight of the verse is on what Christ did for him. Nothing in it says he'll turn around and judge you.

explanations.answer: He must learn to eat everything
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. What he says about the brother is, “…your brother, for whom Christ died.” Nothing in the verse tells that brother to learn to eat everything. The weight of the verse is on the fact that Christ died for him.

Paul says the opposite. Verse 17 reads, “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.” So the kingdom isn't about what's on the plate. It's about righteousness, peace and joy.

Right. Verse 17 says, “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.” The kingdom isn't a menu. It's righteousness, peace and joy, and I'd say that's a better thing to chase.

explanations.answer: What leads to peace and builds each other up
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 19 says, “So then, let us pursue what leads to peace and to mutual edification.” Mutual edification means building each other up. It's a trade: you stop trying to win, and you start trying to build.

explanations.answer: Whatever proves which side is right
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. He says, “…let us pursue what leads to peace and to mutual edification.” The goal is peace and building each other up. Winning the argument isn't on his list.

explanations.answer: Strict rules for every meal they share
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't tell them to do that. What they pursue is “…what leads to peace and to mutual edification.” He has already said the kingdom isn't a matter of eating and drinking. A rulebook for every meal would be pretty far from that.

Yes. Paul says, “All food is clean, but it is wrong for a man to let his eating be a stumbling block.” He holds both halves together. The food is clean, and it is wrong to let eating be a stumbling block.

Paul does say it. Verse 20 reads, “All food is clean, but it is wrong for a man to let his eating be a stumbling block.” He gives the food a clean slate and still cares about the brother. Both ideas sit in the same sentence.
Yes. Verse 21 says, “It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or to do anything to cause your brother to stumble.” The point is the brother. If it would cause him to stumble, you give it up.

That isn't the pair Paul names in this verse. He says it's better not to “…eat meat or drink wine or to do anything to cause your brother to stumble.” The things in the verse are meat and wine. Feasting and fasting aren't mentioned.

Paul doesn't mention singing or praying aloud. He says, “It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or to do anything to cause your brother to stumble.” The two named things are meat and wine. That's a very different list.

Yes. Verse 22 says, “Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves.” It's a blessing for the person whose conscience is clear about what he does. Most of us could use a clear conscience about the last cookie.
Praise sounds nice, but Paul's word is condemn. He says, “Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves.” The blessing is for the person whose choice doesn't turn on himself.

Forgiving is a good thing, but Paul's word here is condemn. He says, “Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves.” The blessing goes to the person whose own conscience stays clear about what he does.

explanations.answer: His eating is not from faith
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 23 says, “But the one who has doubts is condemned if he eats, because his eating is not from faith…” The problem isn't what's on the plate. He's doubting while he eats. That's the part Paul points to.

explanations.answer: The food is unclean in itself
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite. In verse 14 he says, “…nothing is unclean in itself.” and in verse 20 he says, “All food is clean…” The condemnation in verse 23 comes because “…his eating is not from faith…” It's about the doubt, not the food.

Paul doesn't give that reason. Verse 23 says he's condemned “…because his eating is not from faith…” Giving thanks came up earlier in verse 6, but it isn't the reason here. The reason is that he's acting against his doubts.
Yes. The last words of the chapter are, “…everything that is not from faith is sin.” It ends the chapter on faith. I think that's what holds the whole chapter together.

Paul does end that way. The last words of verse 23 are, “…everything that is not from faith is sin.” The chapter closes on faith. That's easy to lose track of after all those verses about food, days, judging and giving an account.
